text: AI-generated answers are now part of how people search. When a prospective customer asks Google a question, they may see an AI-generated answer before they’re given a list of websites. And they might even choose to use an AI platform like ChatGPT to get answers or perform tasks. The reality is that AI search changes how brands gain visibility and get customers. To stay competitive, you need generative engine optimization to appear in AI-generated responses. In this guide, we explain what generative engine optimization is, how it relates to SEO, and how to approach it strategically. What Is Generative Engine Optimization? Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the practice of optimizing your presence and content to appear in responses generated by AI-powered search systems such as ChatGPT, Google, Perplexity, Claude, and others. Instead of focusing solely on search engine rankings (i.e., SEO ), GEO is about becoming part of the output that AI systems deliver—known as agentic search . Agentic search can include collecting and retrieving sources to answer a user's question, or completing a task on their behalf, like making a purchase (also called agentic commerce ). For example, when I asked Perplexity which VPN service is best, it pulled information from multiple sources across the web and synthesized it into a comprehensive answer. The response included an overall recommendation with key details, a table that compared a few options, and suggested follow-up questions. The key difference between SEO and GEO is that you aren’t competing to rank at the top of search results in GEO—you’re competing to be part of the final output. SEO vs. GEO SEO focuses on helping you appear in search engine results pages (SERPs), while GEO focuses on helping you appear within AI-generated answers. And much of the SEO work you’re already doing is equally important for increasing visibility within the agentic web . That said, here’s a breakdown of some of the ways SEO and GEO differ. SEO GEO Goal Optimizes for search rankings Optimizes for agentic search Key tactics Ensuring crawlability, incorporating keywords, aligning with search intent, and building backlinks Writing with clarity and extractability in mind, getting mentioned by credible sites and platforms, and keeping content fresh Metrics Keyword rankings and organic traffic AI visibility , AI mentions, AI citations , and AI share of voice Why Does GEO Matter? GEO matters because AI-powered search shapes what people see—and what they buy. ChatGPT hit 100 million users faster than any app in history. Google’s AI Overviews now reach billions of users each month. What this means is that people now turn to AI for product recommendations, research, and comparisons. AI systems are able to act as sales representatives to influence purchasing decisions, and some can even make purchases on your behalf. If AI-generated answers mention your brand or product, you become part of the consideration set. If they don’t, you may not be seen at all by potential buyers. Here are some more specific benefits of investing in GEO: You can gain organic visibility without paying for ads You can attract qualified traffic Your brand can be surfaced in results 24/7 Your brand becomes credible in your industry Generative Engine Optimization Strategies The strategies that make you visible in search rankings overlap significantly with the ones that get you mentioned in AI answers. SEO is all about creating great content, making it accessible to search engines, and building quality backlinks . The top generative engine optimization strategies for AI visibility are to consistently publish content around topics closely tied to your brand, make your content easy to access and understand, and earn credible mentions across the web. Basically, AI assistants want to provide helpful, accurate information to users the same way search engines do. And they pull that information from the same internet your SEO-focused content lives on. The more your brand is associated with the topics you care about, the more likely it is to be referenced in an AI-generated answer (generally). For marketers, the message is that you don’t need to abandon your SEO strategy to build your presence in AI engines. SEO and GEO work together. And separating them into two distinct strategies might not make sense. As SEO export Aleyda Solís points out, tools that simply show you where your brand appears in AI answers aren’t enough on their own (as seen with the shutdown of GEO startup Lorelight): Instead, brands should focus on how to integrate AI-search insights into a broader search strategy that includes SEO.So, if you've been doing solid SEO for years, you're already much of the way there with GEO. To perform generative engine optimization, publish relevant content consistently, make your content accessible to AI crawlers, and earn brand mentions from other sources. Microsoft's official guidelines for generative search reinforce this: make your catalogs machine-readable, structure content to answer real questions, and establish authority through credible sources and expertise signals. These are the same principles that drive SEO success. We’ll probably see more tactics that help specifically with appearing in AI systems in the future, especially as we better understand how they retrieve, interpret, and synthesize information. Based on what we’ve learned so far, there are a few specific ways you can optimize for AI systems: Unlinked brand mentions seem to carry more weight. AI systems may give brand mentions more weight even when they’re not linked. This is a kind of a big deal because even casual mentions of your brand across the web could boost your AI visibility. Content with quotes and statistics tends to perform well in AI assistants . One study analyzed 10,000 real-world queries and found that pages containing quotes and statistics had 30%-40% higher visibility in AI responses compared to content without them. Server-side rendering might be important for AI visibility . AI crawlers seem to have trouble executing JavaScript, so your content might be invisible if it relies heavily on client-side rendering. Which means it might not get picked up, processed, or included in AI-generated responses. Fresh content is often favored by AI tools . AI tools want to provide the most current information possible. Wikipedia presence could potentially boost your AI visibility . Since Wikipedia seems to make up a significant portion of AI training data, having an accurate Wikipedia entry for your brand might increase the likelihood of being mentioned in AI responses. UGC platforms appear to influence generative engine visibility . Platforms that allow user-generated content (UGC)—Reddit, YouTube, Facebook, etc.—appear to have high exposure in generative engines. So brand presence on these platforms could be important. A Mindset Shift for Marketers For decades, marketers optimized for clicks, rankings, and SERP features . Now, visibility also means being cited, summarized, and recommended inside AI-generated responses. But that doesn’t mean the need for strong SEO has disappeared. Many SEO best practices are still relevant. Now, visibility often means showing up inside the answer and where AI systems retrieve information from. So you need to start tracking how often AI is actually mentioning you and pulling from your content as a source in addition to your standard SEO tracking. SEO aims to improve your visibility in organic search results. GEO aims to improve your appearance in AI-generated answers. Most brands need both for a comprehensive search visibility strategy. Are There Risks to Generative Engine Optimization? The primary risk of GEO is optimizing for AI at the expense of human readers. Content overloaded with quotes, statistics, or prompt-heavy formatting without real value won’t perform well long term. AI visibility can also fluctuate as platforms evolve. The safest approach to GEO is to focus on publishing accurate, helpful content and engaging in brand-building tactics. Is Generative Engine Optimization the Future of Digital Marketing? GEO is already part of the digital marketing conversation, but it doesn’t replace other marketing efforts. SEO, social media marketing, email marketing, paid ads, etc., are still important. text: Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the practice of making your website easy for AI answer engines, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews, to find, understand, trust and cite. Classic SEO earns a position in a list of links. GEO earns a place inside the answer itself: your brand named, your facts quoted and your page linked as a source. This guide is the hub for everything we have published on GEO. It explains how AI engines choose sources, how GEO differs from SEO and AEO, what to change on your pages and how to measure the result. Key Takeaways GEO builds on SEO. A page that AI crawlers cannot reach, or that search engines do not index, will not be cited however well it is written. AI engines quote passages, not whole pages. A direct, self-contained answer under each heading is the single most useful change you can make. Evidence wins citations. In the original GEO research, adding statistics, quotations and cited sources raised visibility in AI answers by up to 40%. Entity clarity matters as much as content. Your company, products and authors need one consistent set of facts across your site, structured data and public profiles. Measure with a fixed set of buyer prompts: how often you are mentioned, how often you are cited and whether the answer describes you correctly. What Is Generative Engine Optimization? A generative engine is a search or assistant product that writes an answer instead of only listing links. It retrieves pages, reads them and summarizes what it found, usually with a handful of cited sources. Generative engine optimization is the work of becoming one of those sources. The term comes from a 2023 research paper, GEO: Generative Engine Optimization , by researchers from Princeton University, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi, later presented at the KDD 2024 conference. The authors tested how different content changes affected a page's visibility inside AI generated answers. Adding relevant statistics, quotations from credible sources and citations performed best, improving visibility by up to 40% in their benchmark. Keyword stuffing, the old SEO shortcut, did little or nothing. In practice, GEO covers three jobs: letting AI systems reach your pages, making your pages easy to quote accurately and giving the engines enough evidence to trust you over a competitor. For definitions of the terms used in this guide, see our AI search and GEO glossary . Why Does GEO Matter Now? Buyers increasingly ask an assistant before they search. In February 2024, Gartner predicted that traditional search engine volume would drop 25% by 2026 as people turn to AI chatbots and virtual agents. Google itself now shows AI Overviews and AI Mode above or instead of the familiar results for many queries. Two things follow for a marketing team. First, a page can rank well and still be absent from the AI answer for the same question. Second, the answer often names only three to five brands. Being one of them is worth more than ranking seventh, and being left out means the buyer may never see your link at all. How Do AI Engines Choose Which Sources to Cite? Each product works differently, but most follow the same broad pattern, often called retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): Retrieve. The engine turns the question into one or more searches. Google describes a "query fan-out" technique for AI Mode, where one question becomes many related sub-queries. Only pages the engine can crawl and has indexed can be retrieved. Read and select. The model reads the retrieved passages and keeps those that answer the question directly, agree with other trusted sources and come from a site it can identify. Write and cite. The model writes its answer from the selected passages and links some of them as sources. That pattern explains most of GEO. If you are not retrievable, nothing else matters. If your answer is buried in the fifth paragraph of a long introduction, a competitor's clearer passage gets picked. If your facts conflict with what other sites say about you, the engine may leave you out or describe you wrongly. We go deeper into the selection step in How Do LLMs Choose Sources to Cite? GEO vs SEO vs AEO: What Is the Difference? The three overlap heavily. The difference is mainly where you want to appear and how you measure success. Discipline Goal Where you appear What it rewards Main measure SEO (search engine optimization) Rank in search results Google and Bing result pages Relevance, links, technical health, page experience Rankings, organic clicks AEO (answer engine optimization) Be the direct answer Featured snippets, voice assistants, AI Overviews Concise answers to specific questions, structured data Snippet and answer ownership GEO (generative engine optimization) Be named and cited in AI written answers ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, Copilot, AI Overviews and AI Mode Retrievable, quotable passages, evidence, consistent entity facts Mention rate, citation rate, answer accuracy The practical takeaway: you do not need three separate programs. Good technical SEO is the foundation, AEO habits make your answers quotable and GEO adds evidence, entity clarity and a new way to measure. The Five Foundations of GEO 1. Access: Let AI Systems Reach Your Pages Check that robots.txt allows the crawlers you want, including search engines and AI retrieval agents such as OpenAI's OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot . Also check your CDN or firewall, which can block these bots even when robots.txt allows them. Serve the main content in the HTML rather than only through JavaScript, keep XML sitemaps current and use IndexNow to tell Bing and other participating engines when pages change. Note that Google's Google-Extended token controls use of your content for Gemini model training and grounding, and Google states it does not affect inclusion in Search, including AI Overviews. 2. Entity Clarity: Make It Obvious Who You Are AI engines build answers around entities: companies, products, people and places. Describe your company the same way everywhere, with the same name, location, founding year, offering and numbers. Publish Organization, Product or SoftwareApplication and Person structured data in Json-ld , and link your official profiles with sameAs. Give every author a profile page with a real name and role, and link articles to it. 3. Answer-First Content: Write Passages Worth Quoting Start each page with a one or two sentence answer to its main question. Phrase headings as the questions buyers actually ask, then answer each one in the first 40 to 60 words beneath it before adding detail. Define terms in a single sentence. Use tables for comparisons and numbered lists for steps, because both are easy to lift into an answer without losing meaning. Our 12-point GEO checklist turns this into a page-by-page review. 4. Evidence: Give Engines a Reason to Trust You Specific, sourced facts are what the GEO research found most effective. Add statistics with their source and year, quote recognized experts, link to primary sources and, above all, publish first-party data that no one else has: results from your own projects, benchmarks from your own platform and case studies with measured outcomes. A page that only restates what ten other pages say gives an engine no reason to cite it. 5. Freshness and Trust: Keep Facts Current and Honest Show a visible published date and, when you revise a page, an updated date that matches your structured data. Change that date only when the content genuinely changes. Remove or update statistics that have gone stale, keep prices and product facts in one place and follow Google's guidance on helpful, reliable, people-first content , which AI features draw on as well. Which On-Page Elements Matter Most for GEO? Element Why AI engines use it Where to start Direct answer under each heading It is the passage most likely to be quoted Your top 10 commercial and help pages Question-style headings They match how people phrase prompts Rewrite vague headings like "Overview" Tables and numbered steps Structure survives summarization intact Comparisons, pricing models, processes Sourced statistics and first-party data Evidence makes a passage more citable Case studies and pillar guides JSON-LD structured data It states entities and relationships explicitly Organization, product, author and article markup Named authors with profiles They show who stands behind the claims Every article and guide Visible, accurate dates Engines prefer current information Articles and anything with numbers FAQs written as real questions Each one is a ready-made question and answer pair Service, product and pillar pages How Do You Measure GEO? Rankings do not tell you whether AI engines mention you, so GEO needs its own measures. Build a fixed set of 30 to 100 prompts your buyers really ask, across awareness, comparison and purchase questions, and run them on a regular schedule in the engines that matter to you. Then track: Mention rate: the share of prompts where your brand appears in the answer. Citation rate: the share of prompts where one of your pages is linked as a source. Share of voice: your mentions compared with named competitors on the same prompts. Accuracy: whether the answer describes your products, prices and facts correctly. AI referral traffic: visits from domains such as chatgpt.com and perplexity.ai in your analytics, and what those visitors do next. Answers vary from run to run, so look at trends over several weeks rather than single results. Our guide to AI visibility checkers explains these metrics in detail, and conversion rate optimization for AI search traffic covers what to do once those visitors arrive. A 90-Day GEO Plan Days 1 to 15, baseline: write your prompt set, record current mention and citation rates, and audit crawler access, indexing and structured data. Days 16 to 30, foundations: fix crawler and rendering issues, add Organization, product and author markup, publish author profiles and make your company facts consistent across the site and your public profiles. Days 31 to 60, content: rewrite your 10 most important pages answer-first, with question headings, a table where it helps, sourced statistics and genuine FAQs. Days 61 to 90, evidence: publish at least one piece of first-party data or a detailed case study, link it from related pages, then rerun your prompt set and compare against the baseline. How We Apply GEO at Cyberdunes We run this site on the same principles we recommend, so you can inspect every item yourself: Our robots.txt names AI search, user-triggered and training crawlers in separate groups, so each policy can be changed on its own, and we review it quarterly. Our llms.txt and llms-full.txt files are generated from the same page data the site renders, so the facts they give language models never drift from the pages. Every page is prerendered to plain HTML and carries one linked JSON-LD graph: the organization, the Apex ® product, the page, its breadcrumb, its author and its FAQs. Articles name a real author with a profile page, and sitemap dates come from when a page actually changed, not from the last deploy. The same capabilities are built into Apex ® , our AI-native digital experience platform, which tracks how AI engines describe your brand and helps you fix the gaps. If you would rather have a team do the work, our GEO services start with a visibility review of your site and buyer prompts. Common GEO Mistakes to Avoid Blocking AI crawlers by accident through CDN bot protection or a copied robots.txt. Hiding content behind JavaScript that crawlers may not run. Stuffing keywords instead of answering the question; the GEO research found it ineffective. Bumping dates without changing content , which undermines trust in every date you publish. Templated FAQ filler that repeats the page instead of answering new questions. Inconsistent facts between your site, your structured data and your public profiles. Measuring only rankings , which misses whether AI engines mention you at all. text: AI Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Generative engine optimization matters because the audience has already moved: 49% of US adults now use AI chatbots, up from 33% in 2024, and 60% say they read AI summaries in search results (Source: Pew Research Center). Your buyers are asking ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews before they ever see a list of links. That changes the goal. Ranking on page one still matters, but it no longer guarantees you appear in the answer. The work now is getting your brand, your data, and your pages cited inside the response itself. This guide covers what GEO is, how it relates to SEO and AEO, how engines choose sources, the tactics that move citations, and how to measure a channel that often hides its wins. Key Takeaways GEO earns citations inside AI answers, not positions in a list. Strong SEO is still the entry ticket for AI visibility. Statistics, quotes, and cited sources raise citation odds. AI referral traffic is small but tends to convert well. Track citation share, not just clicks. What Generative Engine Optimization Means Generative engine optimization is the practice of structuring content, entities, and off-site signals so AI systems select your pages as sources and cite or mention your brand in their answers. The term comes from a 2024 study by researchers at Princeton, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI, and IIT Delhi. They tested optimization methods across 10,000 queries and found targeted changes could lift a source’s visibility in generated answers by up to roughly 40%. Adding quotations, adding statistics, and citing sources were among the strongest moves. Keyword stuffing did close to nothing. Here is the difference from classic SEO in one table: SEO GEO Goal Rank in a list of results Be cited inside the answer Main signal Relevance plus backlinks Clarity, evidence, entity trust Unit of competition The page The passage Success metric Rankings and clicks Citation share and mentions Typical win A visit A recommendation, often without a click SEO, AEO, GEO, and AIO: How the Layers Stack The acronyms multiply fast. A useful way to keep them straight is to treat them as layers, each built on the one below. SEO makes you discoverable. Crawlability, indexation, site architecture, relevance, and authority. If a page cannot be crawled or is not trusted, no generative engine will use it as a source. Weak SEO leaves GEO with nothing to work on. Authority makes you trusted. Editorial, contextual links and mentions from real publications still signal that other people find your content worth referencing. Quality beats volume. One mention in a respected industry outlet does more than fifty directory links. AEO makes you extractable. Answer engine optimization is about structure: direct answers near the top, question-style headings, clean passages a machine can lift without losing meaning. GEO makes you citable. This is the layer that decides whether an engine actually picks your passage when it synthesizes an answer from several sources. Some teams add AIO (AI optimization) for machine usability: structured data, consistent templates, fast and accessible pages. It amplifies what already works. It cannot rescue a weak foundation. The practical order follows from that: fix SEO, build authority, structure for extraction, then optimize for citation. Why GEO Went Mainstream in 2026 Three shifts pushed GEO from experiment to budget line. The interface changed. Conductor found AI Overviews on about a quarter of the queries it tracked in early 2026 (Source: Conductor), and AI assistants now sit inside browsers, phones, and work tools. Clicks dried up. Roughly 68% of US Google searches ended without a click in the first months of 2026 (Source: SparkToro). An answer that satisfies the user keeps them on the results page. The traffic that does arrive is valuable. AI referrals still account for only about 1% of website visits overall, but closer to 3% for IT and technology sites, and ChatGPT sends the large majority of them (Source: Conductor). Those visitors usually arrive mid-decision, having already read a summary that named you. Small volume, high intent. How Generative Engines Choose Their Sources Most AI search products follow the same basic loop. They interpret the question, often fanning it out into several sub-queries. They retrieve candidate pages and passages from a search index. Then they synthesize an answer and attach citations to the sources that supported specific claims. You win at the retrieval and synthesis steps. Engines tend to favor: Direct, early answers. A passage that resolves the question in its first two sentences is easy to quote. Verifiable specifics. Numbers, dates, named sources, and concrete examples. Clear entities. Consistent naming of your company, products, and people across your site and the wider web. Topical depth. Several related pages covering a subject, not one isolated post. Freshness. Recently updated pages for anything time-sensitive. Corroboration. Claims that match what other credible sources say. Off-site signals carry real weight. If third-party publications, comparisons, and reviews mention your brand , engines see corroboration they cannot get from your own site alone. The Tactics That Move Citations Seven moves account for most of the gains. Lead every section with a self-contained answer Write the first one or two sentences under each heading so they make sense on their own, out of context. That is exactly how an engine will use them. Add statistics, quotes, and sources This is the tactic the original GEO research found most reliable. Use current, attributable numbers from neutral sources, quote named experts, and say where every figure comes from. Phrase headings as real questions Match the way people prompt: “How long does GEO take to work?” beats “Timeline considerations.” Pull questions from sales calls, support tickets, and the “People also ask” box. Strengthen entity signals Use one consistent brand name. Keep an accurate About page, author bios with real credentials, and schema.org markup (Organization, Article, FAQ, Person) in JSON-LD. Make sure titles, meta descriptions, and alt text describe the page plainly. Build topic clusters Cover a subject from several angles and link the pages together. Engines read clusters as topical authority, and fan-out queries are more likely to land on one of your pages. Refresh on a schedule Update statistics, dates, and examples on your highest-value pages every quarter. Stale numbers are an easy reason for an engine to pick a competitor. Earn third-party mentions Get included in the comparison articles, listicles, and review pages that engines already cite for your category. Look at which URLs appear in AI answers for your target prompts, then pitch those publishers. Digital PR and original research are the most durable ways to do this. None of this replaces technical basics. Page speed, mobile usability, crawlable rendering, and clean information architecture still decide whether you make the candidate list at all. Measuring a Channel That Hides Its Wins GEO often produces no click. A buyer reads an answer that names you, then types your URL into the browser a week later. Analytics files that under direct traffic. Call it the dark funnel. Mature programs measure three layers: Citation share. For a fixed set of high-intent prompts, how often is your brand mentioned or your page cited, compared with competitors, across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, and Google’s AI features? Mention quality. Is the description accurate? Is the sentiment positive? Is the AI repeating outdated pricing or a competitor’s framing? Downstream behavior. Sessions, engagement, and conversions from AI referrals, plus lifts in branded search and direct traffic. Citations are volatile. You can hold a spot for weeks and lose it overnight after a model update. Track monthly, look at trends rather than single runs, and expect recovery to take several weeks. If you need software for this, see the best AI visibility tools for 2026 . The Honest Caveats GEO is real, but keep it in proportion. Absolute traffic is still small for most sites, so treat GEO as an extension of SEO, not a replacement. Measurement standards are immature, and different tools will report different citation shares for the same prompts. Be skeptical of vendor ROI claims you cannot reproduce. And platform economics can shift quickly. New link formats, ads inside AI answers, or a change in which index an assistant uses can reshape the channel within a quarter. There is also a naming trap. “GEO audit” sometimes refers to local, geographic SEO (map listings, NAP consistency). That work matters for local businesses, but it is a different discipline from generative engine optimization. Check which one a vendor means before you sign. How to Get Started in Four Weeks Week 1: audit. Write 20 questions a buyer would actually ask. Run them through ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google’s AI experience. Record who gets cited, which URLs, and whether you appear at all. Week 2: retrofit. Pick your five most valuable pages. Add answer-first openings, question headings, current sourced statistics, and schema. Week 3: earn mentions. List the third-party pages engines cited in your audit. Pitch inclusion, offer data or expert commentary, and update your own profiles on the platforms that show up. Week 4: monitor. Set up monthly prompt tracking for those 20 questions, including competitor citation share. If you would rather hand this off, compare options in the top GEO companies and the best AEO companies , and ask every agency how they measure citations before you look at pricing. Conclusion Generative engine optimization is what visibility looks like when people get answers instead of links. You still need the SEO foundation and real authority, but the deciding factor is whether your content is clear, specific, and corroborated enough for an engine to quote it. Start small and measurable. One week of prompt testing will show you exactly where you stand against competitors, and a handful of rewritten pages plus a few well-placed third-party mentions is usually enough to see citations begin to move within a couple of months. Read Next Go deeper on AI search and brand discovery: Brand Mentions and AI Search: How Startups Get Cited by ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Overviews Brand Presence in the Age of AI and Search AI-Powered Search Is Changing the Way Customers Discover Brands Frequently Asked Questions What is generative engine optimization? Generative engine optimization is the practice of making your content and brand more likely to be cited or mentioned in AI-generated answers from tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google AI Overviews. It focuses on clear answers, verifiable evidence, strong entity signals, and third-party mentions. How is GEO different from SEO? Generative engine optimization builds on SEO but measures success differently. SEO aims to rank pages in a list and win clicks. GEO aims to have specific passages selected and cited inside a synthesized answer, often without a click at all. What is the difference between GEO and AEO? GEO and AEO overlap heavily. AEO, or answer engine optimization, focuses on structuring content so machines can extract a direct answer. GEO focuses on being chosen and cited by generative AI systems, which also depends on authority, evidence, and off-site mentions. How long does generative engine optimization take to work? Generative engine optimization can show early citation changes within roughly two to three months on pages that already rank and get crawled often. Gains from new third-party mentions and topic clusters usually take longer. Results vary by engine and can swing after model updates. Does generative engine optimization drive traffic? Generative engine optimization drives a small but valuable stream of traffic. AI referrals are around 1% of visits for most sites, higher in technology categories, and those visitors often arrive further along in their decision. Much of the impact shows up as branded and direct traffic rather than tracked referrals.

text: GEO, short for Generative Engine Optimization, is the set of measures that make sure AI search engines can find your website, understand it and cite it as a source in their answers. Think of ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot and Google AI Overviews. Where SEO is about a place in a list of ten links, GEO is about a place in a single written answer. This guide gives you the full overview. Each part has its own in-depth article with examples and steps. If you come across a technical term, you'll find it explained in the GEO glossary . # What exactly is GEO? GEO is optimising your website and content so that large language models use your information and refer to you when they answer a question. The term comes from research by Aggarwal and colleagues at Princeton University, Georgia Tech, the Allen Institute for AI and IIT Delhi. In 2023 they described GEO as a new field and studied which changes to a text increase the chance that a generative search engine uses it. In practice, GEO has three goals: Access. The crawlers of AI services are allowed to read your pages, and are able to. Understanding. The system grasps who you are, what you offer and which facts belong to you. Citation. Your text is so reliable and well structured that an AI system chooses it as a source and links to you. You'll come across other names too. AEO (Answer Engine Optimization) covers the same idea. Some people talk about LLM optimisation or AI SEO. Flowproof uses GEO because it is the most established term and the research is named after it. # Why GEO matters now GEO matters because a growing share of search queries is answered by an AI system that writes its own answer instead of showing a list of links. Google shows AI Overviews and AI Mode above or instead of the classic results. ChatGPT and Perplexity search the web live and give an answer with a few source citations. For you as a website owner, that changes the rules of the game. In a list of ten results, position six can still bring in visitors. In an AI answer with three sources, you are either in it or invisible. On top of that, some users no longer click through after reading the answer (a zero-click search). If you are mentioned, that counts as brand awareness. If you are not, the answer often mentions your competitor instead. So GEO doesn't replace your SEO work. It builds on it and shifts the emphasis from rankings to citations. # GEO and SEO: what is the difference? The difference between GEO and SEO lies mainly in the goal and the way you measure it: SEO aims for a high position in the search results, GEO aims to be mentioned in a generated answer. The foundation is largely the same. A page that can't be crawled, loads slowly or lacks clear information performs poorly in both. Google itself says you don't need separate optimisation for its AI features on top of good SEO. SEO GEO Goal High position in the search results Being mentioned and cited in an AI answer Measure of success Ranking, clicks, organic traffic Mentions, citations, traffic from AI platforms Unit Page and keyword Passage, fact and entity Key signals Relevance, links, technical setup, user experience The same, plus quotable wording, unambiguous facts and access for AI crawlers Measurement Search Console, rank tracking tools Prompt tests, referral traffic, specialised monitoring tools Where exactly they overlap and differ, and where to spend your time first, is covered in the article on the difference between GEO and SEO . # How AI search engines choose sources AI search engines use two kinds of knowledge: what the language model learned during training, and what it looks up live at the moment of the question. That live lookup is called retrieval . The system sends out one or more searches, fetches pages and then writes an answer based on what it found. Anchoring an answer in sources it has found is called grounding . For AI Mode, Google describes a technique called query fan-out : one question is split into several sub-questions, each of which is searched separately. A page that clearly answers one sub-question therefore stands a chance, even if it doesn't rank for the main question. This leads to two practical lessons for GEO: For live answers, your current website counts. If your page is crawled today and is clear, it can appear in an answer next week. For knowledge inside the model, your reputation and mentions elsewhere count. You build these more slowly, through good content, mentions on other sites and consistent information about your brand. How this works per platform, which crawler belongs to which service and what makes a passage quotable is explained in the article on how AI search engines choose sources . # The four steps to an AI answer A website only ends up in an AI answer if it passes four steps: access, understanding, trust and conversion. If one is missing, the steps after it fall away. The best content won't help if the crawler is blocked. Step The question What you set up Further reading 1. Access Is the AI crawler allowed and able to read your page? robots.txt, firewall, server-side rendering, sitemap AI crawlers in robots.txt and llms.txt 2. Understanding Does the system grasp who you are and what you offer? Structured data, clear headings, unambiguous facts Schema markup for AI 3. Trust Is your page a reliable source? E-E-A-T, sources, freshness, author Content that AI cites 4. Conversion Does the visitor from the answer become a customer? Clear CTA, social proof, fast page Flowproof free scan, CRO section Flowproof scans exactly these four steps across nine sections. The rest of this guide follows the same order. # Access: let AI crawlers in The first requirement for GEO is that the crawlers of AI services are allowed to visit your website. You give that permission in robots.txt . Many sites block AI bots without realising it, for example through a general rule, a plugin or a security setting at their hosting provider. The most important distinction is between search bots and training bots . OpenAI, for example, has several : OAI-SearchBot indexes pages so they can be shown in ChatGPT's search feature. ChatGPT-User fetches a page when a user asks for it in a conversation. GPTBot collects content that may be used to train models. If you block GPTBot, ChatGPT can still mention you in search answers, as long as OAI-SearchBot is welcome. If you block OAI-SearchBot, you disappear from those answers. Google works differently. AI Overviews use the regular Googlebot. With the Google-Extended token you only control whether your content may be used for Gemini models. Watch your firewall too. A CDN or security service can refuse AI bots while robots.txt allows them. You won't see that in robots.txt, only by sending a request with the user agent of such a bot. A full overview of all AI bots, example files and the firewall test is in the article on AI crawlers in robots.txt . # llms.txt: a reading guide for language models llms.txt is a Markdown text file in the root of your website that briefly tells language models what your site is and where the most important information can be found. The idea was proposed in 2024 by Jeremy Howard on llmstxt.org . The file starts with a title, a one-line summary and then sections with links to your key pages. You need to be honest about its effect: it is a proposal, not an official standard. Google's John Mueller said in 2025 that it plays no role in Google Search. Other companies and documentation platforms do offer it. Because it takes little effort and has no downsides, it is a reasonable addition. It doesn't replace robots.txt, structured data or good content. How to build one, with a full example and the pitfalls when publishing, is covered in the article on llms.txt . # Understanding: make facts unambiguous with schema markup Schema markup is structured data in your page's code that tells machines in a fixed format what something is: an organisation, a product, an article or a frequently asked question. The most widely used format is JSON-LD , a block of code in the head of your page. For GEO, the principle of entities matters most. An AI system needs to know that "Flowproof" on your site is the same company as the profile on LinkedIn and the entry in the company register. With the Organization type and the sameAs field you make that connection explicit. The types that make the difference for most business websites: Organization or LocalBusiness : name, logo, address, contact details and sameAs. WebSite and BreadcrumbList : the structure of your site. Article with author and dates: who wrote what, and when. Product and Offer : prices and offers, important for shopping features in AI search engines. FAQPage : questions and answers that match exactly how people ask. Which types to use when, with a full JSON-LD example and how to validate it, is in the article on schema markup for AI . # Trust: write content that AI cites Content that AI cites answers a question directly, backs up its facts and shows who is behind the information. Google sums up its quality criteria as E-E-A-T : Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness and Trustworthiness. Google describes these principles in its guidance on helpful, reliable content . They also fit well with what AI systems choose as a source. What you do in practice: Answer first. Start every section with a sentence that fully answers the question, even without the surrounding context. That is the sentence an AI system can lift. Headings as questions. Phrase headings the way your customer would ask ChatGPT. Facts with sources. Mention specific numbers, dates and names, and link to the original source. Structure. Lists, step-by-step plans and tables are easy to process and are often reused. Freshness. Show the date the page was last updated and keep it honest. Author. Show who writes the content and why that person or organisation knows the subject. A detailed approach with a before-and-after example and a checklist is in the article on content that AI cites . # The technical basics that often get forgotten A common reason for being invisible in AI answers is that a page's text only appears after JavaScript has run in the browser. Many AI crawlers run no JavaScript, or only a limited amount. They then see an empty page. With server-side rendering or pre-rendering, your text is right there in the HTML the server sends. Also check these points: Speed. Crawlers don't wait forever. An HTML page that arrives within about a second is a safe guideline. Sitemap. An up-to-date XML sitemap, referenced in robots.txt, helps crawlers find your pages. Indexability. A forgotten noindex keeps a page out of search engines, and therefore also out of AI answers that rely on those search engines. Language. A lang attribute on the page states which language and market your content is meant for. Canonical. For similar pages, a canonical tag indicates which version is the original. # How do you measure GEO? You measure GEO with a combination of prompt tests, traffic from AI platforms and your existing SEO data, because there is no generally available "Search Console for ChatGPT" yet. Choose ten to twenty questions your customers ask and test them monthly in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Mode. Note whether your brand is mentioned and whether your site is linked. In your web analytics you can also see how many visitors arrive via domains such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai. Search Console remains important for the basics: a page that isn't indexed won't show up in AI Overviews either. There are specialised platforms that track mentions in AI answers at scale. Flowproof deliberately focuses on what you can improve on your own website. That's why it makes sense to use technical checks and citation monitoring side by side. # Common GEO mistakes The most common GEO mistake is a website shutting out AI crawlers without the owner knowing. That happens through an overly broad rule in robots.txt or through a security setting that is switched on by default. The second is content that is accurate but written in such a way that no single sentence can be quoted on its own. The table lists the mistakes Flowproof sees most often in scans, with the fix. Mistake Consequence Fix Blocking all AI bots as a precaution You also disappear from the search features of ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude, not just from training Make a distinction: allow search bots and decide consciously what to do with training bots Robots.txt is open, but the firewall blocks Bots get an error while everything seems fine Test with an AI bot's user agent and adjust your bot management Text is loaded only with JavaScript Crawlers without JavaScript see an empty page Server-side rendering or pre-rendering No Organization markup or sameAs AI can't link your brand to your profiles elsewhere Add Organization or LocalBusiness with sameAs Introductions that only get to the point after three paragraphs There is no sentence that gives the answer in one go Start every section with the answer Claims without a source or date Lower reliability, less chance of being cited Link to primary sources and show an update date Anonymous content No demonstrable expertise Show author, team and about-us information GEO as a one-off project Outdated pages and broken links after a few months Schedule a quarterly review of scan, prompts and content # What GEO is not GEO is not a way to trick AI systems. Hidden text for bots, text posing as instructions to a language model, or pages stuffed with repeated keywords work against you. Search engines and AI platforms recognise manipulation, and Google classes techniques like these as spam . GEO is also no substitute for a good product or good service. An AI system that weighs up reviews and mentions elsewhere also sees what customers say about you. # Step-by-step plan: how to get started with GEO Start with GEO by sorting out technical access first, then making your key pages unambiguous, and only then working on new content. In this order you get the most out of your time: Scan your website for access, structure and content, so you know where you stand. Check robots.txt and at the very least allow the search bots of OpenAI, Perplexity, Anthropic and Microsoft. Test your firewall with an AI bot's user agent. Set up bot management so that the bots you allow actually get in. Check that your text is in the HTML without JavaScript being needed. Add Organization or LocalBusiness markup , with sameAs pointing to your main profiles. Rewrite the opening sentences of your five most important pages so they answer the main question directly. Make it clear who you are : about us, team, contact details and authors on articles. Publish an llms.txt listing your key pages. Record a baseline with ten prompt tests and your current traffic from AI platforms. Repeat every quarter : scan again, test the prompts and update outdated pages. # How to check this on your own site You can check most points in this guide yourself with your browser, your robots.txt and a structured data validator. It's quicker with a scan that checks everything in one go. Flowproof's free scan looks at your site the way an AI crawler does. It checks twelve AI bots in robots.txt, tests whether your firewall lets GPTBot through, reads your llms.txt and schema markup, and gives concrete advice for each finding. Then start with the section that has the lowest score and work through the steps in this guide from top to bottom.

text: The brands showing up in AI search results didn’t crack an algorithm. They built a presence that AI systems can find, understand, and trust. In other words, exactly what generative engine optimization (GEO) helps you do. As large language models (LLMs) change how people discover information and make decisions, GEO is how you ensure your brand and content show up in AI-generated answers. That’s a bigger deal than it sounds. Search has moved well beyond Google in 2026. We’re in the “Search Everywhere” era, where users seek information across platforms. And among them, AI platforms are one of the fastest-growing discovery channels of all. Research from Semrush predicts that LLM traffic will overtake traditional Google search by the end of 2027. Our own data suggests that’s likely to be true. In just three months, we saw an 800% year-over-year increase in referrals from LLMs. We’re seeing tens of millions of additional impressions in Google Search Console as AI Overviews reshape how Google displays answers. The brands that adapt now will be in a much stronger position to stay visible as this shift continues. In this guide, I’ll explain: What GEO is and how it’s different from SEO Why you shouldn’t throw away everything you’ve already learned The top techniques that will help you optimize your content for generative engines (and drive results for your business in the process) Free resource: Download our GEO Audit Checklist to work through every step I discuss in this guide. What Is Generative Answer Optimization (GEO)? Generative engine optimization is the practice of ensuring AI systems can find, understand, and reference your brand and content in their answers across platforms. It’s a holistic approach that includes: Publishing content in the right places where AI platforms are most likely to discover it Earning positive brand mentions across the web, even without direct links Ensuring technical accessibility so AI crawlers can easily access and understand your content Unlike traditional search, AI platforms go beyond returning a list of links. They pull relevant passages from across the web and use them to compose an answer. Your brand can show up in that answer as a mention, a citation, or both. You’re no longer just optimizing to rank. You’re optimizing to become part of what AI platforms say when your audience asks questions. For example, when I searched “best teleprompter 2026” in ChatGPT, BIGVU appeared directly in the answer, and its site was cited as a source. That’s the kind of visibility GEO aims to create. Why GEO Matters Now Traditional Google search still dominates. It’ll likely continue to drive most of your traffic in the near term. But the way people discover information is changing fast. Success used to mean ranking at the top of the SERP. Looking forward, there may not even be a “top spot.” Instead, you need to become the solution AI platforms include (and recommend) in their answers. The data tells the story: ChatGPT reached 100 million users faster than any app in history (at the time). As of April 2026, it now has more than 900 million weekly users. Month Weekly Users November 2022 1 million January 2023 30 million November 2023 100 million December 2024 300 million February 2025 400 million March 2025 500 million October 2025 800 million February 2026 900 million Google’s AI Overviews now appear on billions of searches every month. Semrush data from 2025 found they show for roughly 16% of all queries, up from just 6.49% at the start of the year. Nearly a third of US consumers used chat-based AI tools for shopping-related tasks by late 2025. Among those under 45, that number jumps to 41%. These numbers point to one thing: generative engines are influencing YOUR audience too. So it makes sense to start optimizing for them now. How GEO and SEO Work Together You might look at this guide and think, “Isn’t this just SEO with a different name?” And honestly? In many ways, it is. But there’s a reason everyone’s talking about it. Terms like GEO, AEO ( answer engine optimization ), and AIO ( AI optimization ) have exploded in interest because they reflect a real shift. And with all the acronyms flying around, it can be tough to know who to listen to. Further reading: SEO vs. GEO, AEO, LLMO: What Marketers Need to Know I’m not saying GEO replaces SEO. But it does help reframe how you think about discovery, which now happens across AI platforms and other surfaces beyond traditional search. Put simply, the job of SEO now looks like this: Evolving From Evolving To SEO = Google Search SEO = multi-surface visibility (Search, AI/LLMs, social) Success = ranking for keywords Success = being found across Search + Chat SEO is a siloed function SEO is cross-functional + connected to product, brand, PR, and social Keyword-first content planning Intent and entity-driven topic planning with semantic structure Backlinks to pass PageRank Traditional backlinks plus more focus on brand mentions and co-citations Traffic as a core KPI Visibility, influence, and conversions across touchpoints as core KPIs Technical SEO as the foundation Technical SEO as the foundation (with additional focus on JavaScript compatibility) The good news is that if you’ve invested in good SEO, you’re already a lot of the way there. GEO builds on the foundation of great SEO: Creating high-quality content for your specific audience Making it easy for search engines to access and understand Earning credible mentions across the web These same elements help AI engines decide which brands to reference. But here’s the difference: AI systems don’t surface information the same way Google does. So some of your tactics and what you track need to evolve. Let’s walk through how to do that. 7-Step Generative Engine Optimization Action Plan We’re still in the early days of understanding exactly how AI engines pull and prioritize content. But one thing is clear: You need to adapt or reprioritize some traditional SEO tactics for generative engine optimization. The first three steps below cover overarching best practices for GEO. Steps 4-7 cover optimizing content for generative engines specifically (and how to track your results). Step 1. Nail the Basics of SEO As I said earlier, good GEO is generally good SEO. But not everything in your broader SEO strategy matters equally for generative engines. I won’t go through every SEO fundamental here. We cover that in our guide to SEO basics . Let’s focus on what matters most. Make Your Site Easy to Read (for Bots) Before AI platforms can reference your content, they need to be able to access and interpret it. So make sure your website is: Crawlable and indexable: If AI platforms can’t access your pages, they can’t reference them in answers Fast and mobile-friendly: Slow, clunky sites hurt UX — and your chances of getting cited Secure (HTTPS): This is now table stakes, and it builds trust with users and AI systems Server-side rendering: Some AI crawlers still struggle with JavaScript-heavy pages, so server-side rendering is often the safer option Show You’re Worth Trusting AI systems are more likely to reference sources that appear credible, identifiable, and well-supported. You can look at this through the E-E-A-T lens: Experience: Share real results, personal use, or firsthand knowledge Expertise: Stick to topics you truly know — and go deep Authority: Get quoted, guest post, or contribute to well-known sites Trust: Use real author bios, cite sources, and include reviews or testimonials Note: I’m not suggesting these AI platforms use an explicit E-E-A-T system. But signals like these still help establish credibility, which makes content easier to trust and reference. Step 2. Build Mentions and Co-Citations AI systems don’t just look at backlinks to understand your authority. They pay attention to every mention of your brand across the web, even when those mentions don’t include a clickable link. That’s because AI systems are built to understand entities, not just content. They try to determine who’s behind the information and whether that entity shows up consistently across the web with clear connections to relevant people, brands, and topics. So your brand needs to exist as a clearly defined entity , with consistent signals across your website, social profiles, and third-party mentions. The more coherent that picture is, the easier it is for AI systems to trust and reference you. Backlinks are still important. But this changes how you should think about building your wider online presence. Audit Your Current Mentions Start by auditing where you’re currently mentioned. Search for your brand name, product names, and key team members across Google, social media, and industry forums. Take note of what people are saying and where those conversations are happening. You’ll probably find mentions you didn’t know existed. Some will be positive, others neutral, and a few might need your attention. Also run your brand name and related terms through the AI platforms themselves. Does Google’s AI Mode cite your brand as a source for relevant terms? Does ChatGPT know who your team members are? What kind of sentiment do the answers have when you ask those platforms about your brand? For a more in-depth sentiment analysis, use Semrush’s AI Visibility Toolkit . It’ll let you track your LLM visibility (a by-product of good GEO) in top tools compared to your rivals: The tool compares your brand to your rivals in terms of AI visibility, market share, and sentiment: And it’ll show you where your brand strengths are and where you can improve: Want to track your brand’s AI visibility? Get a free trial of Semrush One , which includes the AI Visibility Toolkit and Semrush Pro. See how you can compare to competitors across ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI platforms. Keep Building Quality Backlinks Just because mentions are more important than before with GEO, it doesn’t mean you should abandon traditional link building. Backlinks still matter for SEO, and they often lead to the kind of authoritative mentions that AI systems value. But expand your focus beyond just getting links. Further reading: How to Get High Quality Backlinks Aim to Build Co-Citations and Co-Occurrences There are a few different definitions out there of co-citation and co-occurrence. I’ll be honest: the definitions don’t matter as much as the implications. I’ve seen one source define co-citations as the exact thing another source calls co-occurrence. So for this section, I’m just going to talk about what these are and why they matter, without getting bogged down in definitions. The first important way to think of co-citations/co-occurrences is simply the mention of one thing alongside another. In the case of GEO, we’re usually talking about your brand or website being mentioned alongside a different website or topic/concept on another website. For example, if your brand is Monday.com, you’ll pick up co-citations involving: Your competitors (ClickUp, Asana etc.) Key terms or categories associated with your business (like “project management software”) Specific concepts or questions related to what you do (e.g., “kanban boards” and “how to automate workflows”) In Monday’s case, there are hundreds of pages out there that mention it alongside ClickUp and Asana in the context of “project management tools”: This suggests to Google and other generative AI tools that Monday and ClickUp are both related to the term “project management tools” and are both popular providers of this kind of software. The other common way to think about co-citations is mentions of your brand across different, often unrelated websites. For example, Monday being mentioned on Forbes and Zapier would be a co-citation involving them. To sum it up: If two (or more) brands or websites are often mentioned alongside each other, AI systems are more likely to treat them as related (i.e., competitors) If a brand is often mentioned in the context of a particular topic, concept, or industry, AI systems are more likely to associate that brand with those things (i.e., what you offer) If lots of different websites mention a particular brand, AI systems are more likely to see that brand as worth referencing (i.e., probably trustworthy) There’s a lot more to it, but this is a fairly basic overview of what’s going on. How to Put This Into Action To build citations, co-citations, and co-occurrences: Get mentioned alongside competitors: When publications write comparison articles or industry roundups, you want your name in that list. These co-citations help AI systems understand where you fit in your market. Participate in industry research and surveys: When analysts publish reports about your sector, being included gives you credibility (and any backlinks are a bonus). Show up in relevant online communities: Answer questions on Reddit, contribute to LinkedIn discussions, and join industry-specific forums. These interactions create mentions in places where AI systems often look for authentic, community-driven insights. The goal is to become a recognized voice in your space. The more often your brand appears in relevant contexts across the web, the more likely AI systems are to include you in their responses. Step 3. Go Multi-Platform Going beyond Google is something top SEOs have been telling us to do for a long time. But AI has made this an absolute must. Platforms like Reddit, YouTube, and other user-generated content sites appear frequently in AI outputs. In fact, according to Semrush data from January 2026, Reddit and LinkedIn are the two most cited domains across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode. So, a strong brand presence on these platforms could help you show up more often. This helps in at least three ways: Reach your audience where they already are: Being active on multiple platforms lets you meet people where they already spend time. That helps you build engagement, strengthen brand awareness, and drive more conversions. Show up in more AI-referenced places: AI platforms don’t just pull from Google search results. They also draw from forums, social media, YouTube, and other sources beyond traditional SERPs. Reduce your dependence on one channel: A stronger presence across multiple platforms means you’re less exposed to one algorithm, one audience, or one source of traffic. Diversification is just good business practice. Brian Dean did an excellent job of this when he was running Backlinko. That’s why you’ll see his videos appear in Google SERPs for ultra-competitive keywords like “how to do SEO”: We’re taking our own advice here. In fact, it’s a big part of why we launched the Backlinko YouTube channel : Here’s how to put this into practice: YouTube: People go there to learn how to do things, research products, and find solutions to problems. That makes product reviews, tool comparisons, and in-depth tutorials strong candidates for YouTube content . Podcasts: Podcast content and transcripts are beginning to surface in AI results, especially in Gemini. Building a presence here is a good opportunity to gain more AI visibility. TikTok and Instagram Reels: These platforms reach younger audiences who increasingly use them for search. Short-form videos that answer common questions in your industry can drive discovery, and AI platforms can sometimes cite them in responses. Reddit: AI platforms LOVE to cite Reddit for user-generated answers (especially Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode). To grow your Reddit presence , find subreddits where your audience hangs out and share genuinely helpful advice when people ask questions related to your expertise. Don’t promote your business directly. Focus on being useful first. LinkedIn: For B2B topics, LinkedIn can work similarly to Reddit. Publish thoughtful posts and engage in relevant discussions to build your voice in professional circles. Those signals can then get picked up by AI systems looking for expert perspectives. Step 4. Find Out What AI Platforms Are Citing for Your Niche One of the fastest ways to understand what content to create is to study what AI platforms are already citing in your niche. Start by directly testing whether/how your content appears in AI tools right now. Go to ChatGPT, Claude, or Perplexity and ask questions that your content should answer. In the example below, Backlinko is mentioned (great). But there’s also a YouTube video front and center. And forums are appearing too. These are places we might want to consider creating content or engaging with conversations. As you do this for your brand, pay attention to the sources they cite: Are they commonly mentioning your competitors? What platforms do they tend to cite? (Reddit, YouTube etc.) What’s the sentiment of mentions of both your brand and your competitors? Then start testing variations of the same prompt. For example, you could ask, “What’s the best email marketing software?” Then try “Which email marketing tool should I use for my small business?” Notice how the answers change and which sources keep showing up consistently. In the example above, the first prompt mentioned MailerLite, which was absent in the list for small businesses. But the second prompt pushed Mailchimp to the top and mentioned three new options (Constant Contact, Brevo, and ActiveCampaign). If you were MailerLite and trying to reach small businesses, you’d want to understand why you’re not being cited for that particular prompt. Pro tip: Test the same prompts across different AI platforms too. They each have their own citation patterns, so it’s a good idea to compare a few of them. You can automate this process with tools like Profound or Peec AI. These platforms run prompts at scale, helping you understand how and where your brand appears. But they can be expensive. That’s why I recommend you spend some time running these prompts manually at first. By the way: This isn’t just important for “big brands” or those selling products. You can (and should) do this if you run a blog, local business website, or even a personal portfolio. For example, consultants and freelancers will find these tools often cite marketplaces like Upwork and Dribbble. If you don’t have a profile on there, you’ll likely struggle to get much AI visibility. And if you’re a local business owner, you’ll often find specific service and location pages appear in AI responses: This is useful for understanding the types of content you should be focusing on for GEO. Now it’s time to decide what topics to focus on in your content. Step 5. Answer Your Audience’s Questions The way people search with AI platforms is often more conversational than traditional Google search. That changes how you should plan your content. Traditional SEO taught you to target specific keywords. You’d create a page optimized for “healthy meal prep ideas” and try to rank for that phrase. But what happens when people are instead searching for “what to cook for dinner when I’m trying to lose weight”? The answer might involve healthy meal prep as a solution. But it’s a completely different prompt (not a search) that gets to that answer (not a SERP). When you run these queries through Google’s AI Mode, you see two totally different sets of sources and content types. For the “healthy meal prep ideas” query (which is a perfectly valid and searchable term), the focus is listicles, single recipes, and YouTube videos. And the format is categories (bowls, wraps, and sandwiches etc.) with specific recipes: But for “what to cook for dinner when I’m trying to lose weight,” the sources are primarily lists, forum results, or articles specifically around weight loss. In this case, the format of the answer is largely broad tips for cooking healthily and then some general cooking styles or meal types, rather than specific recipes: As more people get comfortable searching in conversational language, longer and more specific queries will become more common. This makes this kind of intent analysis critical. These longer, more specific queries represent huge opportunities. Most companies aren’t creating content that answers these detailed questions. The more specific the question, the more likely you are to show up when AI systems look for credible answers. You want to own the long-tail queries that relate directly to your product or expertise. But: You can’t reasonably expect to create content for every single long-tail query out there. So how do you approach this in an efficient way? How to Choose the Questions to Answer Start by listening to the actual questions your customers ask. Check your customer support tickets, sales calls, and user feedback. These real questions from real people often make the best content topics — because they’re the same kinds of questions people will ask these AI tools. Don’t have any customers? No problem. Use community platforms to find these conversational queries. Reddit, Quora, and industry forums are goldmines for discovering how people actually talk about problems in your space. You can also use Semrush’s Prompt Research tool. Enter a topic (e.g. “healthy meal prep”) and it will show you the exact prompts people are typing into AI platforms. Look especially for question-based prompts. Step 6. Structure Your Content for Generative Engines AI systems process information differently than humans do. They break content into chunks and analyze how those pieces relate to each other. According to Microsoft’s official AEO/GEO playbook Microsoft’s official AEO/GEO playbook, most brands already possess the raw materials: product specs, reviews, FAQs, policies, pricing details. But these assets need to be surfaced and structured for AI systems to see and act on them. An AI that can’t parse your content cleanly will simply move on to another website with better structure. That’s why content structure is one of the highest-level GEO moves you can make. And it doesn’t even require creating anything new. Note: A lot of what I say below is just good writing practice. So while this stuff isn’t necessarily “revolutionary,” these techniques are going to become more important as you focus on GEO. One Idea per Paragraph Keep your paragraphs short and focused on one main idea. When you stuff multiple concepts into a single paragraph, you make it harder for AI systems to extract the specific information they need. Also avoid burying important information in the middle of long sentences or paragraphs. Front-load your key points so they’re easy to find and extract. And guess what? It also makes it easier for your human readers to understand too. So it’s a win-win. Use Clear Headings Use clear headings and subheadings to organize your content logically. Whatever your heading says, the content under it should deliver on that immediately. Don’t drift. AI systems use headings to understand what each section covers. If the content doesn’t match, that section is harder to extract and cite. For example, look at the headings in this section. Then read the first sentence under each one. Notice how they’re all clearly linked? This is a common technique when trying to rank for featured snippets. You’d have an H2 with some content that immediately answers the question… …and this would rank for the featured snippet for that query: This is still a valid strategy for traditional search. But for GEO, you need to have this mindset throughout your content. I’d also recommend against making every H2 a question. That will quickly start to look over-optimized. Just make sure the content under each heading clearly and logically delivers on what the heading says. Break Up Complex Topics into Digestible Sections If you’re explaining a complex or multi-step process, use numbered steps and clear transitions between each part. This makes it easier for AI systems to pull out individual steps when someone asks for specific instructions. And it also makes the process easier for readers to follow. Also write clear, concise summaries for complex topics. AI systems often look for these kinds of digestible explanations when they need to quickly convey information to users. Use Quotes, Statistics, and Clear Statements Include quotes, statistics, and clear statements that AI systems can easily extract. Because pages with quotes or statistics have been shown to have 30-40% higher visibility in AI answers. So instead of saying “Email marketing could be an effective channel for your business,” write “Email marketing generates an average ROI of $42 for every dollar spent.” Note: Don’t just flood your content with quotes and stats. Only include them when they add value and genuinely help your readers. Use Schema Markup Schema markup can help AI systems understand who you are, what your content is about, and how to interpret it correctly. But just remember: it’s not a magic potion for AI visibility. Google’s official AI search guide states that structured data isn’t required for generative AI search, and there’s no special schema type that unlocks AI Overview inclusion. The independent data backs that up. A large-scale Ahrefs study found that pages with schema are cited more often by AI tools — but adding schema to already-cited pages didn’t make any significant difference . The correlation reflects overall site quality, not schema’s direct effect. Use schema because it’s solid SEO practice — not because you expect it to unlock AI citations. Well-built sites get cited. Here are a few schema types worth prioritizing: Organization schema: Helps establish who is behind the site and gives AI systems clearer identity signals about your brand HowTo schema: Helps define the sequence of actions in a step-by-step process more clearly FAQ schema: Adds structure to Q&A content that AI platforms may find easier to interpret and extract Date schema: Helps AI systems assess when content was published (“datePublished”) and last updated (“dateModified”) After implementing the schema, validate it at validator.schema.org to make sure it’s working correctly. You don’t need to be a developer to do this. Most CMS platforms, including WordPress, have plugins that can generate the markup for you automatically. Make It Scannable Use formatting like bold text to highlight important facts or conclusions and make your content easier to skim. This helps readers quickly find key points. And it can also make important information easier for AI systems to identify. Scannability has always been a big focus at Backlinko. We use lots of images to convey our most important points and add clarity through visualizations: We use clear headings to make our articles easy to follow: And if you look at this article as a whole, you’ll see the same principle in action. Clear headings, short paragraphs, bullets, bolded lead-ins, and visual breaks make the content easier to scan and follow. The goal is to make your content easy to read and navigate for humans and machines. Well-structured content typically performs better across all types of search and discovery. Step 7. Track Your Visibility in LLMs AI visibility isn’t a metric you check once. Which brands get mentioned, which sources get cited, and how your brand is described can all shift significantly over time. That means monitoring needs to be ongoing. Tracking your visibility in AI-generated responses helps you understand what’s working and where you need to focus your efforts. But where do you start? And what should you track? Manual Testing as a Starting Point Start with manual testing. This is the simplest way to see how you’re performing right now. Ask the same questions across different AI platforms, like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Google (both AI Mode and AI Overviews). Take screenshots of the responses and note which sources get cited. Do this regularly, and you’ll start to see patterns in which types of content get mentioned and how your visibility changes over time. Honestly though: you’re going to struggle to get a lot of meaningful data doing this manually. It’s not scalable. And so much of what an AI platform outputs depends on prior context, including: Past conversations Previous prompts within the same conversation Project or chat settings A study by SparkToro proved this inconsistency. They ran 12 prompts across ChatGPT, Claude, and Google AI Mode nearly 3,000 times. The study found that AI tools produce the same brand recommendation lists less than 1 in 100 times, and identical ordering less than 1 in 1000 times . That means the right question isn’t “where do I rank in ChatGPT?” because there is no clear rank. The right question is: “How often does my brand appear across a meaningful sample of prompts?” Which is exactly what makes it hard to gather truly reliable data on your own. Manual tracking is really more of a “feel” test that is best treated as a rough directional check, not a complete tracking system. Use AI Tracking Tools You can start with a free AI visibility checker for quick, top-level insights and see where your brand currently stands. For ongoing checks, add your questions to Semrush’s Prompt Tracking . It requires an AI Visibility Toolkit subscription. Check the Sources report to see which pages the answers cite, including your own. Tools like Semrush Enterprise AIO help you track your brand’s visibility across multiple AI platforms like ChatGPT, Claude, and Google’s AI Overviews. It shows you exactly where you stand against competitors and gives you actionable steps to improve. Another option is Ziptie.dev. It’s not the most polished tool yet, but they’re doing some really interesting work — especially around surfacing unlinked mentions across AI outputs. The key here: don’t treat AI tracking like keyword rank tracking. You don’t need to monitor thousands of prompts to see where you show up. Instead, pick 10-20 representative prompts that reflect how your audience searches. Run them regularly across platforms in your AI tool fo choice, and track your mention rate over time. That directional signal is far more meaningful than any “AI ranking” your tools might report. Why Talk to Your Boss (or Clients) About GEO? You’ve seen the steps. Now you need a story. GEO gives you a simple way to explain what’s changing in search without making it sound like everything you knew about SEO suddenly stopped working. It helps you say: Traditional SEO still matters Past investments in content and authority still count But visibility now means more than rankings alone Your brand also needs to be cited, mentioned, and trusted in AI-generated answers That makes it easier to get buy-in, justify your strategy, and keep moving forward without having to rebuild your entire approach from scratch. You Need to Start Now to Stay Visible This space is evolving fast. New capabilities are rolling out monthly. But the brands showing up consistently in AI search aren’t chasing every new development. They’re building something durable: content, presence, and trust signals that AI systems are designed to find and reference. Start with the basics by continuing to optimize for strong rankings and authority. Then grow your presence by adding the GEO layer on top of your SEO efforts. And keep tracking your AI visibility as you go. Download our free GEO Audit Checklist . It covers all seven steps I discussed in one place so you can work through them systematically. Also, check out our video with Backlinko’s founder , Brian Dean. We dive into how search habits are changing and how you can build a resilient, multi-channel brand. Backlinko is owned by Semrush.
